items.title: Who gets to tell a worker's story?
items.dek: Lee Chang-dong's first film in eight years sets a laid-off factory worker beside a documentary-maker who wants his story. Speaking to Little White Lies, the Korean director turns the film's central question on himself.
paragraphs: Eight years is a long silence for a director of Lee Chang-dong's stature, but the South Korean filmmaker has never worked to a schedule. His new feature, Possible Love, his first since the 2018 thriller Burning, premiered in competition at the Venice Film Festival in September, had its North American premiere in Toronto and began a limited theatrical run on 23 October ahead of its worldwide release on Netflix on 6 November. In a conversation with David Jenkins for Little White Lies, published on 22 October, Lee talks less about craft than about a question that has shadowed him since he wrote fiction: what right does an artist have to someone else's suffering?

The film is built around two married couples on either side of a class divide. Ho-seok, played by Sul Kyung-gu, is a former factory worker who has never recovered from losing his job after a strike; his wife Mi-ok, played by Jeon Do-yeon, works at a carwash and meets the world with stubborn optimism. Across the divide stand Ye-ji, an aspiring documentary filmmaker played by Cho Yeo-jeong, and her wealthy husband Sang-woo, played by Zo In-sung. Ye-ji is developing a project about displaced workers, and Ho-seok's story is exactly what she has been looking for.

Lee told Jenkins that the project began roughly a decade ago, after a large Korean conglomerate laid off many of its workers. He shelved it because a documentary about those workers already existed, and found his way back only when his co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, suggested adding the filmmaker couple. That detail is revealing. The story became possible for Lee only once it included someone like him: an outsider with a camera and good intentions, who stands to gain from another person's loss.

The film's politics of work are unusually explicit. Lee argues that labourers in particular tend to build their sense of self through what they do, so that the erosion of stable employment strips away identity as well as income. He also suggests that the distance between the rich and the struggling has grown so wide that the phrase class gap no longer seems adequate, while insisting that the film should still affirm the basic equality of its characters and the longing for freedom that might carry them beyond their circumstances. A recurring whistle stands in the film for the tacit solidarity among workers and for labour handed down from parent to child, which Lee describes as both painful and sacred.

Yet Lee is careful not to turn Ye-ji into a villain or the documentary into a target. He told Jenkins that he is not suspicious of documentary as such; in his account, Ye-ji stands for anyone who makes a living from other people's stories, novelists and directors included. His criticism is aimed at a broader habit of art: the way it can feed on the pain of marginalised people without passing that pain on truthfully. Whether he is worthy of a given story, he says, is a question that has followed him since his years as a novelist, and one he has never been able to set down.

What follows is interpretation rather than reporting. That reflexive turn places Possible Love in a long tradition of films about the ethics of looking, but it lands with particular force at a moment when precarious lives are routinely converted into content. It is hard not to notice that a film about professionals profiting from working-class experience will reach most of its viewers through Netflix, one of the largest streaming platforms in the world; the interview does not dwell on that irony, but Lee's own question invites it. What he offers is not an answer but a discipline: to keep asking, rather than assuming that good politics or good intentions settle the matter in advance.
paragraphs_zh: 对于李沧东这样分量的导演来说，八年是一段漫长的沉默，但这位韩国电影人从来不按时间表工作。他的新片《可能的爱》是继2018年惊悚片《燃烧》之后的首部长片，九月在威尼斯电影节主竞赛单元首映，随后在多伦多举行北美首映，10月23日开始有限院线放映，并将于11月6日在Netflix全球上线。在《Little White Lies》10月22日刊出的与大卫·詹金斯的对谈中，李沧东谈得更多的不是技艺，而是一个自他写小说时起就如影随形的问题：艺术家有什么权利取用别人的苦难？
影片围绕阶级鸿沟两侧的两对夫妻展开。薛景求饰演的浩锡曾是工厂工人，在一次罢工后失去工作，至今没有走出来；全度妍饰演的妻子美玉在洗车场上班，以一种倔强的乐观面对世界。鸿沟另一侧是赵汝贞饰演的有志成为纪录片导演的艺智，以及赵寅成饰演的她富有的丈夫尚宇。艺智正在筹备一部关于失业工人的作品，而浩锡的故事恰恰是她一直在寻找的。
李沧东告诉詹金斯，这个项目大约始于十年前，当时韩国一家大财阀裁掉了大批工人。由于已有一部关于这些工人的纪录片，他把项目搁置了；直到合作编剧吴贞美提议加入那对拍纪录片的夫妻，他才重新找到切入点。这个细节耐人寻味。只有当故事里出现一个像他一样的人——一个带着摄影机和善意的局外人，一个可能从别人的损失中获益的人——这个故事对李沧东来说才变得可能。

影片对劳动的政治态度异常鲜明。李沧东认为，尤其是体力劳动者，往往通过自己的工作建立自我认同，因此稳定就业的瓦解剥夺的不仅是收入，还有身份。他还表示，富人与挣扎者之间的距离已拉得如此之大，“阶级差距”这个说法似乎已不足以形容；但他坚持，影片仍应肯定人物之间基本的平等，以及可能带他们超越处境的对自由的渴望。片中反复出现的一声口哨，象征着工人之间默契的团结，也象征着从父母传给子女的劳动——李沧东形容它既痛苦又神圣。
不过，李沧东小心地避免把艺智塑造成反派，也不把纪录片本身当作靶子。他对詹金斯说，他并不怀疑纪录片这种形式；在他看来，艺智代表所有以讲述他人故事为生的人，小说家和导演也包括在内。他批评的是艺术更普遍的一种习性：它可能以边缘人群的痛苦为养料，却没有真实地把这种痛苦传达出去。他说，自己是否配讲一个故事，这个问题从当小说家时起就一直跟随着他，他始终放不下。

以下是解读，而非报道。这种自我反思让《可能的爱》置身于一个探讨“观看伦理”的悠久电影传统之中，而在不稳定的生活被例行地转化为“内容”的当下，它显得格外有力。人们很难不注意到：一部关于专业人士从工人阶级经验中获利的电影，大多数观众将通过世界上最大的流媒体平台之一Netflix看到它；采访并未细谈这一反讽，但李沧东自己的问题恰恰引人想到这一点。他给出的不是答案，而是一种自律：不断追问，而不是以为正确的政治立场或良好的意图就能预先解决问题。
paragraphs_de: Acht Jahre sind für einen Regisseur von Lee Chang-dongs Rang ein langes Schweigen, doch der südkoreanische Filmemacher hat sich nie nach einem Zeitplan gerichtet. Sein neuer Spielfilm Possible Love, der erste seit dem Thriller Burning von 2018, lief im September im Wettbewerb der Filmfestspiele von Venedig, hatte seine Nordamerika-Premiere in Toronto und startete am 23. Oktober in ausgewählten Kinos, bevor er am 6. November weltweit auf Netflix erscheint. Im Gespräch mit David Jenkins für Little White Lies, veröffentlicht am 22. Oktober, spricht Lee weniger über Handwerk als über eine Frage, die ihn seit seiner Zeit als Schriftsteller begleitet: Welches Recht hat ein Künstler auf das Leid anderer Menschen?

Der Film kreist um zwei Ehepaare auf beiden Seiten einer Klassengrenze. Ho-seok, gespielt von Sul Kyung-gu, ist ein ehemaliger Fabrikarbeiter, der den Verlust seiner Stelle nach einem Streik nie verwunden hat; seine Frau Mi-ok, gespielt von Jeon Do-yeon, arbeitet in einer Waschanlage und begegnet der Welt mit trotzigem Optimismus. Auf der anderen Seite stehen Ye-ji, eine angehende Dokumentarfilmerin, gespielt von Cho Yeo-jeong, und ihr wohlhabender Mann Sang-woo, gespielt von Zo In-sung. Ye-ji entwickelt ein Projekt über entlassene Arbeiter, und Ho-seoks Geschichte ist genau das, wonach sie gesucht hat.

Lee erzählte Jenkins, das Projekt habe vor etwa zehn Jahren begonnen, nachdem ein großer koreanischer Konzern viele seiner Beschäftigten entlassen hatte. Er legte es auf Eis, weil es bereits einen Dokumentarfilm über diese Arbeiter gab, und fand erst wieder hinein, als seine Ko-Autorin Oh Jung-mi vorschlug, das Filmemacher-Paar hinzuzufügen. Dieses Detail ist aufschlussreich. Möglich wurde die Geschichte für Lee erst, als sie jemanden wie ihn enthielt: einen Außenstehenden mit Kamera und guten Absichten, der vom Verlust eines anderen profitieren kann.

Die Politik der Arbeit ist in diesem Film ungewöhnlich deutlich. Lee argumentiert, dass gerade Arbeiter ihr Selbstverständnis oft über ihre Tätigkeit aufbauen, sodass der Verfall sicherer Beschäftigung nicht nur Einkommen, sondern auch Identität raubt. Er meint außerdem, der Abstand zwischen den Reichen und denen, die kämpfen müssen, sei so groß geworden, dass der Ausdruck Klassenunterschied kaum noch genüge – und besteht doch darauf, dass der Film die grundlegende Gleichheit seiner Figuren bejahen solle und die Sehnsucht nach Freiheit, die sie über ihre Lage hinaustragen könnte. Ein wiederkehrender Pfiff steht im Film für die stille Solidarität unter Arbeitern und für Arbeit, die von Eltern an Kinder weitergegeben wird, was Lee als zugleich schmerzhaft und heilig beschreibt.

Dennoch macht Lee Ye-ji nicht zur Schurkin und den Dokumentarfilm nicht zur Zielscheibe. Er sagte Jenkins, er stehe dem Dokumentarischen an sich nicht misstrauisch gegenüber; Ye-ji stehe für alle, die vom Erzählen fremder Geschichten leben, Romanautoren und Regisseure eingeschlossen. Seine Kritik gilt einer allgemeineren Gewohnheit der Kunst: dass sie sich vom Schmerz marginalisierter Menschen nähren kann, ohne diesen Schmerz wahrhaftig weiterzugeben. Ob er einer bestimmten Geschichte würdig sei, sagt er, sei eine Frage, die ihn seit seinen Jahren als Schriftsteller verfolge und die er nie habe ablegen können.

Was folgt, ist Interpretation, nicht Berichterstattung. Diese selbstreflexive Wendung stellt Possible Love in eine lange Tradition von Filmen über die Ethik des Hinsehens, doch sie trifft besonders in einer Zeit, in der prekäre Leben routinemäßig zu Content verarbeitet werden. Kaum zu übersehen ist, dass ein Film über Profis, die aus der Erfahrung der Arbeiterklasse Kapital schlagen, die meisten Zuschauer über Netflix erreichen wird, eine der größten Streaming-Plattformen der Welt; das Interview vertieft diese Ironie nicht, aber Lees eigene Frage legt sie nahe. Was er anbietet, ist keine Antwort, sondern eine Disziplin: weiterzufragen, statt anzunehmen, dass die richtige Haltung oder gute Absichten die Sache im Voraus erledigen.
paragraphs_pt: Oito anos é um longo silêncio para um diretor da estatura de Lee Chang-dong, mas o cineasta sul-coreano nunca trabalhou seguindo um cronograma. Seu novo longa, Possible Love, o primeiro desde o thriller Em Chamas, de 2018, estreou na competição do Festival de Veneza em setembro, teve sua première norte-americana em Toronto e entrou em cartaz em circuito limitado em 23 de outubro, antes do lançamento mundial na Netflix, em 6 de novembro. Numa conversa com David Jenkins para a Little White Lies, publicada em 22 de outubro, Lee fala menos de técnica do que de uma pergunta que o acompanha desde que escrevia ficção: que direito tem um artista sobre o sofrimento dos outros?

O filme gira em torno de dois casais em lados opostos de um abismo de classe. Ho-seok, interpretado por Sul Kyung-gu, é um ex-operário que nunca se recuperou da perda do emprego após uma greve; sua mulher, Mi-ok, interpretada por Jeon Do-yeon, trabalha num lava-jato e enfrenta o mundo com um otimismo teimoso. Do outro lado estão Ye-ji, aspirante a documentarista interpretada por Cho Yeo-jeong, e seu marido rico, Sang-woo, interpretado por Zo In-sung. Ye-ji está desenvolvendo um projeto sobre trabalhadores demitidos, e a história de Ho-seok é exatamente o que ela procurava.

Lee contou a Jenkins que o projeto começou há cerca de dez anos, depois que um grande conglomerado coreano demitiu muitos de seus trabalhadores. Ele o engavetou porque já existia um documentário sobre esses trabalhadores, e só reencontrou o caminho quando sua corroteirista, Oh Jung-mi, sugeriu incluir o casal de documentaristas. Esse detalhe é revelador. A história só se tornou possível para Lee quando passou a incluir alguém como ele: alguém de fora, com uma câmera e boas intenções, que pode sair ganhando com a perda de outra pessoa.

A política do trabalho no filme é invulgarmente explícita. Lee argumenta que os trabalhadores braçais, em especial, costumam construir sua identidade a partir do que fazem, de modo que a erosão do emprego estável lhes tira não só a renda, mas também a identidade. Ele sugere ainda que a distância entre os ricos e os que lutam para sobreviver ficou tão grande que a expressão diferença de classe já não parece suficiente, embora insista que o filme deve afirmar a igualdade básica de seus personagens e o desejo de liberdade que poderia levá-los além de suas circunstâncias. Um assobio recorrente representa no filme a solidariedade tácita entre trabalhadores e o trabalho passado de pais para filhos, que Lee descreve como ao mesmo tempo doloroso e sagrado.

Ainda assim, Lee tem o cuidado de não transformar Ye-ji em vilã nem o documentário em alvo. Ele disse a Jenkins que não desconfia do documentário em si; na visão dele, Ye-ji representa qualquer pessoa que vive de contar histórias alheias, romancistas e diretores incluídos. Sua crítica mira um hábito mais amplo da arte: o modo como ela pode se alimentar da dor de pessoas marginalizadas sem transmitir essa dor com verdade. Se ele é digno de uma determinada história, diz, é uma pergunta que o acompanha desde seus anos de romancista e que ele nunca conseguiu deixar de lado.

O que segue é interpretação, não reportagem. Essa virada autorreflexiva insere Possible Love numa longa tradição de filmes sobre a ética do olhar, mas ela ganha força especial num momento em que vidas precárias são rotineiramente convertidas em conteúdo. É difícil não notar que um filme sobre profissionais que lucram com a experiência da classe trabalhadora chegará à maior parte do público pela Netflix, uma das maiores plataformas de streaming do mundo; a entrevista não se detém nessa ironia, mas a própria pergunta de Lee a convida. O que ele oferece não é uma resposta, e sim uma disciplina: continuar perguntando, em vez de supor que boas posições políticas ou boas intenções resolvam a questão de antemão.

items.grammar: Notice 'only once it included someone like him' and 'found his way back only when...'. 'Only' attached to a time clause (only when, only once, only after) stresses that something happened at that point and not before. If the 'only' clause is moved to the front, the main clause takes inversion: 'Only once it included someone like him did the story become possible.' This fronted form is common in formal and literary writing.
items.grammar_zh: 注意 “only once it included someone like him” 和 “found his way back only when...”。only 修饰时间从句（only when、only once、only after）时，强调事情恰恰在那一刻才发生，而不是之前。如果把 only 从句放到句首，主句要倒装：“Only once it included someone like him did the story become possible.” 这种前置结构在正式和文学性写作中很常见。
items.grammar_de: Achten Sie auf „only once it included someone like him“ und „found his way back only when...“. Steht only vor einem Zeitsatz (only when, only once, only after), betont es, dass etwas erst in diesem Moment geschah und nicht früher. Wird der only-Satz an den Anfang gestellt, folgt im Hauptsatz eine Inversion: „Only once it included someone like him did the story become possible.“ Diese vorangestellte Form ist in formeller und literarischer Sprache verbreitet.
items.grammar_pt: Observe “only once it included someone like him” e “found his way back only when...”. Quando only acompanha uma oração temporal (only when, only once, only after), enfatiza que algo só aconteceu naquele momento, e não antes. Se a oração com only vier no início da frase, a oração principal sofre inversão: “Only once it included someone like him did the story become possible.” Essa forma anteposta é comum na escrita formal e literária.
questions: Why do you think the story only became possible for Lee once a documentary filmmaker entered it?
Lee distinguishes between telling marginalised people's stories and consuming their pain. Where would you draw that line, in film or in other art forms?
Does the fact that Possible Love will mainly be seen on Netflix change how you read its critique? Why or why not?
